body: حسم الجيش الملكي تأهله إلى دور المجموعات من كأس الكنفدرالية الإفريقية لكرة القدم، بعد فوزه على ضيفه كورهوغو الإيفواري بهدفين مقابل هدف واحد، في المباراة التي جمعتهما مساء الأحد بالمجمع الرياضي الأمير مولاي عبد الله بالرباط، برسم إياب الدور التمهيدي الثاني. وافتتح الفريق العسكري التسجيل مبكرا، بعدما حصل على ركلة جزاء في الدقيقة السادسة إثر عرقلة يوسف الفحلي داخل منطقة الجزاء. وواصل الجيش الملكي ضغطه بحثا عن تعزيز النتيجة، لكنه لم يتمكن من استغلال محاولاته أمام المرمى، في المقابل، حاول الفريق الإيفواري الوصول إلى شباك الحارس أحمد رضا التكناوتي دون أن ينجح في ذلك، لينتهي الشوط الأول بتقدم أصحاب الأرض بهدف دون مقابل. ومع انطلاق الشوط الثاني، أدرك كورهوغو التعادل في الدقيقة 54 بواسطة غوتي ديبي، قبل أن يطالب الجيش الملكي بركلة جزاء في الدقيقة 58، عقب تدخل على أحمد حمودان داخل منطقة الجزاء، غير أن الحكم أمر بمواصلة اللعب. وفي الدقيقة 83، تمكن أنس باش من تسجيل الهدف الثاني للفريق العسكري، ليعيد التقدم إلى أصحاب الأرض، ويحسم الجيش الملكي المواجهة لصالحه بهدفين لواحد، مؤكدا عبوره إلى دور المجموعات. المقالة الجيش الملكي يبلغ دور مجموعات كأس الكنفدرالية بعد هزم كورهوغو الإيفواري fمنشورة على جريدة الصباح .

body: حقق الفتح الرياضي أول انتصار له في الموسم الجاري من البطولة الاحترافية، بعدما عاد بالنقاط الثلاث من ميدان نهضة الزمامرة، إثر فوزه عليه بهدف دون مقابل، في المباراة التي احتضنها ملعب أحمد شكري، اليوم الأحد، برسم الجولة الخامسة. وانتظر الفريق الرباطي الدقيقة الـ63 لحسم المواجهة، حين نجح أمين صوان في هز شباك أصحاب الأرض، مانحا فريقه هدفا ثمينا. وقبل ذلك، لم تسفر محاولات الفريقين خلال الشوط الأول عن أي تغيير في النتيجة، إذ فرض الحارسان محمد فرني وأيوب لكرد حضورهما بتدخلات ناجحة حالت دون اهتزاز الشباك، لينتهي النصف الأول من اللقاء بالتعادل دون أهداف. ومع انطلاق الشوط الثاني، تواصلت محاولات الجانبين بحثا عن هدف السبق، إلى أن استثمر الفتح الرياضي إحدى فرصه ليتقدم في النتيجة، قبل أن يضغط نهضة الزمامرة في الدقائق المتبقية لإدراك التعادل، دون أن يتمكن من تغيير النتيجة. وبهذا الفوز حقق الفتح الرياضي أول انتصار له هذا الموسم، فيما أخفق نهضة الزمامرة في استغلال عاملي الأرض والجمهور للخروج بنتيجة إيجابية. المقالة الفتح الرياضي يفوز على نهضة الزمامرة fمنشورة على جريدة الصباح .

body: حسم المغرب الفاسي تأهله إلى دور المجموعات من دوري أبطال إفريقيا لكرة القدم، بعدما عاد بانتصار ثمين من قلب أبيدجان على حساب مضيفه أسيك ميموزا الإيفواري بهدفين لواحد، في المباراة التي جمعتهما اليوم بملعب فيليكس هوفويت بوانيي، ضمن إياب الدور التمهيدي الثاني من المسابقة. ووجد الفريق الفاسي نفسه متأخرا في النتيجة خلال الشوط الثاني، بعدما تمكن باكاري كيفن من منح التقدم للفريق الإيفواري في الدقيقة 63، ليصبح المغرب الفاسي مطالبا بتدارك الموقف وانتزاع بطاقة العبور خارج قواعده. ولم يتأخر رد ممثل الكرة المغربية، إذ نجح الكونغولي كريستوفر إيباي في إدراك التعادل في الدقيقة 73، معيدا المواجهة إلى نقطة الصفر، قبل أن تتواصل المحاولات بحثا عن هدف يحسم نتيجة اللقاء. وبينما كانت المباراة تتجه نحو نهايتها، نجح خالد بابا في تسجيل هدف الانتصار في الدقيقة 97، مانحا المغرب الفاسي فوزا ثمينا بعدما قلب تأخره إلى انتصار في الأنفاس الأخيرة. المقالة المغرب الفاسي يتأهل إلى دور مجموعات دوري الأبطال بعد الفوز على أسيك ميموزا fمنشورة على جريدة الصباح .

body: أوقفت الشرطة الإقليمية في كاتالونيا 128 شخصا في برشلونة، ليلة الأحد، للاشتباه في تورطهم في أعمال تخريب وإلحاق أضرار بالممتلكات العامة ونهب متاجر، من بينهم 73 قاصرا، ستحال ملفاتهم على نيابة الأحداث. وقالت سيلفيا كاتا، قائدة شرطة كاتالونيا، في تصريح لمنصة “3 كات إنفو” الإعلامية، إن 15 عنصرا من الشرطة أصيبوا خلال الأحداث، مضيفة أن اثنين فقط من الموقوفين سبق أن كانت لهما سوابق جنائية. وأظهرت تسجيلات متداولة على شبكات التواصل الاجتماعي مجموعات من الشباب، ارتدى عدد كبير منهم ملابس سوداء، وهم يهاجمون متاجر في برشلونة، بعدما تجمعوا وسط المدينة للمشاركة في مسيرة لم يسبق الإبلاغ عنها لدى السلطات. وأوضحت كاتا أن الدعوة إلى التجمع انتشرت عبر مواقع التواصل الاجتماعي، رغم أن الحراك لم يكن منظما، ووصفت ما وقع بأنه “عنف مجاني لا مبرر له”، مشيرة إلى أن الشرطة تعمل على دراسة الملفات الشخصية للموقوفين. وتأتي هذه الأحداث في سياق اضطرابات شهدتها بلدان أوروبية أخرى، من بينها فرنسا وإيطاليا وألبانيا، تخللتها أعمال نهب وعنف. المقالة إيقاف 128 شخصا في برشلونة إثر أعمال تخريب وإصابة 15 شرطيا fمنشورة على جريدة الصباح .

body: At nearly 10 feet (3 meters) tall and around 500 pounds (230 kilograms), Gigantopithecus was the largest primate that ever lived. Foraging across the dense tropical forests of Southeast Asia between 2 million and 200,000 years ago, the giant ape may have shared the habitat with new arrivals — hominins such as Homo erectus . (Hominins are members of the group that includes modern humans, their ancestors and closely related species, after the evolutionary split from great apes.) Despite their immense size Gigantopithecus mainly consumed plants and is closely related to modern-day orangutans. So what would have happened when Gigantopithecus encountered these human ancestors? Experts suggested a variety of possible scenarios, including that Gigantopithecus and human ancestors didn't encounter each other at all. body: The largest artificial intelligence (AI) firms increasingly understand that they are hostages of one another. If one firm pushes ahead recklessly, others may feel compelled to follow. If one deploys a dangerous model without adequate safeguards, others may see it as a green light to do the same. The debate over AI has centered on what governments should do to regulate this frontier technology. That remains essential. But a more immediate question is emerging: Can the companies building these powerful systems take action independently before they lose credibility and suffer legal consequences? That question no longer looks theoretical and is being recognized as an urgent challenge. We've already seen AI firms lose control of their models — for example, in Australia, a rogue AI hacked a government healthcare website . title: Watch the full 'Hunter's Moon' rise next to Saturn this weekend
summary: You'll have two chances to see October's full Hunter's Moon rise dramatically this week. Here's when to get the best views.
body: October's full "Hunter's Moon" is about to rise, and skywatchers will get two great chances to see it appear on the eastern horizon around sunset. Although it officially turns full at 12:11 a.m. EDT on Monday (Oct. 26), the Hunter's Moon will appear almost perfectly full as it rises on both Sunday (Oct. 25) and Monday evenings, giving skywatchers two opportunities to observe it. October's full moon is nicknamed the Hunter's Moon because it was traditionally a signal for hunters to prepare for the coming cold winter by hunting, slaughtering and preserving meat, according to Time and Date . That's an Anglo-Saxon name; Native American names for October's full moon include the Drying Rice Moon, the Falling Leaves Moon and the Freezing Moon. summary: New observations from the James Webb Space Telescope reveal a concentration of heavy metals near the Milky Way's central black hole. The discovery deepens a mystery about why our galaxy's black hole behaves the way it does.
body: The Milky Way's supermassive black hole is surrounded by a surprising trove of heavy metals, according to new observations by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The metals may offer new clues about how Earth got its share of heavy elements — but it could also make one of the greatest mysteries about our local black hole even harder to solve. In astronomy , metals refer to any element heavier than hydrogen or helium, with common examples including oxygen, carbon, iron or gold. These elements are forged through nuclear fusion in the hearts of stars that are reaching the ends of their lives, before being sprayed into space and incorporated into new generations of stars. Scientists say the material spotted by JWST likely came from supernovas ‪—‬ stellar explosions that blasted the metal into the region around Sagittarius A (Sgr A*), the monster black hole in the middle of our galaxy. The coin is inscribed with the name of the Norwegian king Olaf Haraldsson, who ruled from 1015 to 1028 and, as St. Olaf or "Olaf the Holy," is considered the national saint of Norway. Fewer than 20 coins minted during Olaf's reign have ever been discovered, and the newfound coin is a "national treasure," according to a statement from the University of Oslo's Museum of Cultural History. "Here we have a coin bearing the king's portrait and a cross, with another cross on the reverse," University of Oslo coin expert Svein Gullbekk said in the statement. title: Lightest known pair of neutron stars proves Einstein right yet again
summary: Einstein's theory of relativity just got put to the test by the lightest binary neutron star system ever discovered.
body: Astronomers have discovered the lightest known pair of neutron stars — two ultradense stellar remnants that circle each other every 2 hours, 22 minutes, veering toward an inevitable collision about 82 million years from now. By timing radio pulses from one of the stars, the researchers detected three subtle effects predicted by Albert Einstein 's general theory of relativity and found that the theory describes the pair's motion to within about 1% — proving the visionary physicist right yet again . The researchers published their findings Sept. 15 in the journal Physical Review Letters . Neutron stars are the collapsed cores of massive stars that exploded as supernovas. Each packs more mass than the sun into a ball roughly 12 miles (20 kilometers) in diameter. Some, called pulsars, spin rapidly and sweep beams of radio waves across the sky like cosmic lighthouses. Their rotation is so steady that their pulses work as extraordinarily precise clocks. Very few pulsars orbit another neutron star. body: In the late 1800s, Westminster Abbey clergy stumbled upon a mysterious sarcophagus. For nearly 150 years, the tomb has baffled experts, but the abbey's consulting archaeologist may have finally figured out who was buried there, according to a new study. Westminster's chief mason unearthed the stone sarcophagus in 1869, but when experts investigated it, they discovered that the burial had been looted earlier that century. Experts also noticed that the carved decoration on the side of the sarcophagus was stylistically Roman , with a Latin inscription that can be translated as "To the memory of Valerius Amandinus. title: Could 'body clocks' play a role in depression? Study proposes a new 'circadian' subtype
summary: Researchers propose a new subtype of depression linked to body-clock patterns.
body: Some people with depression sleep far more than average, wake up exhausted, habitually stay up late, and experience mood shifts with the seasons. A new study suggests that these symptoms may cluster in a distinct subtype of depression that's tied to the body's internal clock. While research has long linked a scrambled circadian rhythm to a risk of mood disorders, neuroscientists are now proposing that these disruptions define a specific form of depression that they call "circadian depression." First conceptualized in 2021 , the body-clock subtype may affect about 1 in 4 people with severe, recurrent or persistent depression, the researchers estimate. In their new study, published Wednesday (Oct. 21) in The British Journal of Psychiatry , the team identified the subtype in about 2,600 people out of over 11,000 evaluated. "Circadian depression is a biologically informed subtype," said study co-author Emiliana Tonini , a neuroscientist at the University of Sydney. "Unlike subtypes defined mainly by symptoms, the core feature here is a disturbed circadian system, which common antidepressants may not fully address," Tonini told Live Science in an email. body: The mysterious and undeciphered Voynich manuscript has caused consternation among code-breakers, linguists and scholars of medieval literature for more than a century. But now experts think they've worked out why it's so hard to crack: It was bound incorrectly in the 15th century, meaning the pages are out of order. The new linguistic analysis of the document has moved researchers closer to figuring out what the text was all about. The Voynich manuscript is a medieval codex made up of leaves of parchment carbon-dated to the early 15th century. Its 240 pages are covered with about 38,000 words of a unique script called "Voynichese" along with illustrations of people, plants and astrological symbols. Also known as the Beinecke Cipher manuscript, the document was initially owned by a Holy Roman emperor and was purchased by Wilfrid Voynich in 1912. Since 1969, the manuscript has been in the collection of Yale University's rare book library . Experts have unsuccessfully tried to decipher the manuscript for more than a century. body: Stimulating the brain with ultrasound could help counter the delusions people experience in schizophrenia, a small trial finds. The trial involved transcranial ultrasound stimulation, in which a device placed on a patient's head delivers ultrasound waves through the skull and into the brain. Its goal is to change the activity in a targeted brain region. Delusions are false beliefs that are very difficult to shake; for example, a person might believe they are being stalked when they aren't or think that a major disaster is about to occur without any evidence to suggest so. In the trial, researchers found that a 10-minute session of the ultrasound treatment reduced the severity of delusions for at least a week in patients with schizophrenia or a related disorder. summary: The Orionid meteor shower peaks overnight on Oct. 21-22. Here's how to see "shooting stars" from Halley's Comet.
body: One of the best fall meteor showers peaks this week, when pieces of the famous Halley's Comet streak across Earth's atmosphere as fast-moving "shooting stars." The Orionid meteor shower will peak overnight Wednesday (Oct. 21) through Thursday (Oct. 22), potentially producing around 20 meteors per hour under a dark sky, according to Time and Date . The Orionids are caused when Earth passes through the debris left by Halley's Comet, which last passed through the inner solar system in 1986 and will return in 2061 . Halley's Comet is presently beyond the orbit of Neptune, according to The Planets Today , but it doesn't need to be close to Earth to cause "shooting stars." Every time the comet travels through the inner solar system, heat from the sun causes it to shed dust and rocky particles along its orbital path. Earth's own orbit takes the comet through streams of that ancient debris several times a year, with the particles vaporizing as they slam into our planet's atmosphere. summary: A gene variant called APOE4 is the biggest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease. Scientists are finally figuring out how it works.
body: A gene variant called APOE4 dramatically increases the risk of late-onset Alzheimer's disease, the most common form of dementia. Now, emerging research is revealing APOE4's true role in the condition, and a new study pinpoints a possible way to treat it. Historically, scientists studying Alzheimer's disease have focused on two proteins that accumulate in patients' brains: amyloid-beta and tau. However, there's a "third thing that people didn't pay attention to, until recently," said study co-author Li-Huei Tsai , a neuroscientist at MIT. That third thing is the accumulation of droplets of fat, or lipids, in the brain, she told Live Science. The APOE gene makes proteins responsible for transporting fat around cells throughout the body and brain. A version of the gene called APOE4, which increases the risk of late-onset Alzheimer's three- to 12-fold, makes proteins that are less efficient at this function, Tsai said. But how APOE4 affects different brain cells was not clearly understood. Tsai's team has been working to close that gap for about a decade. summary: Researchers have found that during the Black Death, when a third of Europe's population was wiped out, biodiversity fell. Understanding the farming practices of the time could help us increase diversity in modern agriculture.
body: When millions of people died in Europe during the Black Death, biodiversity suffered too, new research suggests. The findings suggest that human activities once promoted biodiversity in the landscape — and experts say we could use these findings to boost biodiversity in our modern agricultural landscapes. The 14th century was a tumultuous time for the people of Europe. Persistent cold, wet weather at the beginning of the century led to widespread agricultural failures and unprecedented levels of starvation in what became known as the Great Famine from 1315 to 1317. This was followed by the Black Death , an epidemic of bubonic plague caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis that killed more than a third of Europe's population. As a result of the widespread deaths and resultant social upheaval, large swaths of agricultural land were abandoned. Population levels didn't begin to recover until the 16th century . title: Can cuttlefish hypnotize their prey?
summary: Cuttlefish use rapid color-change while hunting. The question is, does it actually hypnotize their prey?
body: Like their cephalopod cousins the octopuses , cuttlefish are masters of disguise. As they hunt, these marine predators send waves of color across their skin. The rainbow display stops prey in their tracks, granting the cuttlefish just enough time to shoot out two specialized hunting tentacles at lightning speed and snatch them into range of their deadly beaks. But can cuttlefish actually mesmerize prey with their colorful skin changes? Or is something fishier at play? Experts told Live Science that cuttlefish are ingenious hunters, but that there's likely an even more mysterious process than hunter to prey hypnosis going down on the seafloor. A calculated hunter Cuttlefish are visual hunters , using their large, complex eyes to locate and track potential meals. In general, their strategy involves a slow, stealthy approach, said Bret Grasse , the manager of cephalopod operations at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole Massachusetts. title: California redwoods are struggling in the heat — and it's not clear how much damage is being done
summary: When temperatures rise, California redwoods slow down their rate of photosynthesis, a discovery that could have implications for the long-term survival of the iconic species.
body: When temperatures spike, California redwoods slow down photosynthesis, new research has found. This finding has serious implications for the long-term survival of the iconic trees in a warming world, and their role in storing carbon from the atmosphere. California redwood ( Sequoia sempervirens ) forests are among the largest aboveground carbon stores on the planet. These towering trees are native to central and northern California , and evolved to take advantage of the region's historically mild weather . In recent decades, their range has contracted significantly . But climate change is threatening the health and function of these forests. The region has seen significant warming in recent decades, and faces more frequent extreme heat days , with temperatures spiking above 100 degrees Fahrenheit (37 degrees Celsius). Now, in a new study, published Sept. 22 in the journal JGR Biogeosciences , a team of researchers has shown that California's renowned redwoods are struggling to photosynthesize in the heat. summary: A recent study may reshape our understanding of brain evolution and open new avenues for studying neurological diseases.
body: Recent research challenges a long-standing idea about how the brain develops: Rather than arising from a single source, the brain may emerge from two distinct populations of cells, the study finds. "The brain appears as one organ," said study co-author Kyle Loh , an associate professor of developmental biology at Stanford University. "However, we discovered that the front part of the brain and the back part of the brain come from different sources, which are pushed together to create the appearance of a single organ," Loh told Live Science in an email. The findings, published in September in the journal Nature Neuroscience , not only challenge established models of how the brain forms but may also explain why researchers have struggled to grow certain types of brain cells in the laboratory. The scientists say the work could offer new ways to investigate diseases that affect the brainstem, the "stalk" that connects the brain to the spinal cord. title: New 4,300-mile-long internet cable will shuttle data along the ocean floor at 1 million gigabits per second
summary: Petal, the world's first petabit transoceanic fiber cable, could theoretically support simultaneous music streaming for 75% of the world's population.
body: A new 4,300-mile (7,000-kilometer) undersea fiber cable will shuttle data between the U.S. and France at breakneck speeds of up to 1 million gigabits per second (Gbps) — enough to move around 125 terabytes of data every second, or roughly 25,000 HD movies, each 5 gigabytes large. The cable, called Petal, will be funded and operated by Facebook and Instagram parent company Meta. When it comes online in 2029, the ocean-spanning cable will be the first to deliver petabit capacity — double the capacity of existing subsea cables of this length — across transoceanic distances, Meta representatives said in a statement . That's enough to allow 75% of the world's population to stream music at once. Petal will also be the first commercial subsea cable system to use multi-core fiber technology, according to the statement. Whereas conventional fiber strands typically contain a single core, each of Petal's fiber strands will contain two cores that carry optical signals in opposite directions, allowing a single strand to provide the capacity that would conventionally require a pair of single-core fibers. title: Has there ever been a mountain taller than Everest?
summary: Mount Everest may be the king of the planet today, but has Earth ever thrust a larger mountain from its surface?
body: Sometimes, it takes a great struggle to build towering peaks. And what more thunderous event is there than the clashing of continental plates? Geological pileups have birthed some of the largest and tallest mountains on the planet, including Mount Everest and its Himalayan neighbors. But has there ever been a peak taller than Mount Everest, which stands 29,032 feet (8,849 meters) above sea level? The answer is still a mystery, but there are some geological clues about where the tallest peaks would have been in the ancient past, experts told Live Science. Earth's lost mountains Geologists don't have the level of detail required to pinpoint an exact highest peak hundreds of millions of years ago. "We're never going to get that granularity, unfortunately," Alan Collins , a professor of geology at Adelaide University in Australia, told Live Science. However, clues in residual sediments lodged inside Earth's crust hint at the lost grandeur of primordial snowcaps and summits. Scientists study these crusts to understand how deep they went, which can reveal how tall ancient mountains might have been. title: Physicists froze a 'necklace' of atoms — and witnessed a quantum phenomenon predicted 100 years ago
summary: Atoms confined to a single line can bind into clusters called Bethe strings. A new experiment points to a mix of many such clusters, though the evidence is still indirect.
body: "Necklaces" of ultracold atoms have provided new evidence to support a nearly 100-year-old quantum theory. In 1931, physicists were trying to use quantum mechanics to explain why some materials are magnetic. Then, a young physicist named Hans Bethe looked at a single row of electrons. Each electron's spin can point up or down. Bethe worked out the math for how such a row behaves and found that if a few spins in the row flip, they can stick together and travel down the row as a single unit. Decades later, physicists found that Bethe's method also works for larger particles moving along a line , such as atoms. If those particles attract each other, the math predicts they will bind into clusters called Bethe strings. Now, physicists have found evidence of these clusters in a line of ultracold atoms. The findings were published Aug. 29 in the journal Nature Communications . The discovery may not create new gadgets, but it addresses a fundamental mystery in physics. Everything around us, from magnets to phone chips, consists of countless interacting particles. This makes their behavior difficult to predict.
